newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic hands opposition poison chalice.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic hands opposition poison chalice.

text.p: The Belgrade city election commission on Thursday removed the last legal obstacle to the opposition's assuming control over the city by verifying the mandates of the newly elected deputies after months of delay.

Swallowing defeat in 14 of the biggest Serbian cities including Belgrade in November elections must have been hard for President Slobodan Milosevic but he may have handed a poison chalice to his rivals, diplomats said.

Joy over the reinstated results was tempered by the difficulties the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition must conquer to prove itself a credible rival at the vital republic-wide elections later this year.

Western diplomats, whose governments have warned they will be watching closely for any moves to curtail Zajedno's powers, believe the republican authorities will use every trick in the book to discredit the opposition.
The stark reality is that Serbian regional governments can achieve little without the patronage of central authorities, which are exclusively in the hands of the ruling Socialists.
"The regime will introduce all forms of economic pressure and sanctions against us and highlight any failure," Vuk Draskovic, one of the Zajedno leaders warned.
In the cities where it has already assumed control, Zajedno found empty coffers to finance the decaying infrastructure.
"We expected to find a sorry state in the city coffers but were appalled to see just how barren they were," new Nis Mayor Zoran Zivkovic told Reuters.
"There is almost no self-rule now in Serbia. Everything is controlled by the (central) state,"
"What we are in charge of is the waterworks, sewerage and garbage disposal. Our biggest problem is the economy which is under complete control of republican bodies."
Zajedno does not even have power over the police in their towns who report to Milosevic's interior ministry in Belgrade.
The electricity network is also under control of the Serbian government.
Many state-managed companies have had their headquarters transferred to towns safely under the Socialist party thumb.
In effect, Serbian cities must depend on infusions of money from the government.
"This leaves Zajedno extremely exposed to the whim of the (Socialists) and criticism by the state media," a Western envoy said.
"Without foreign aid to boost the local economy and infrastructure and make life better, Zajedno's own voters will turn away from them at the next elections."
But Zivkovic said their next move after taking stock of the depleted city funds and ruined infrastructure was to launch their own marketing campaign for foreign capital abroad.
"We still have some companies which the Socialists did not want. We will try and make them work."

Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader billed as the next Mayor of Belgrade, said if Socialist-run state companies refused to co-operate with the city authorities, he would simply award the job to private companies.
Zajedno leaders said their calls for assistance were politely heard in the West but no promises were made.

"What they should do is get independent experts from abroad who know how to run cities to make an inventory of their needs and then address their grievances to our governments," another western diplomat said.

In an example of possible ways of resisting the republican pressure, the Zajedno mayor of Kragujevac called on his citizens on Thursday to begin civil disobedience after they were handed down tax returns with high interest rates.
He said the republican authorities owed Kragujevac citizens since March more than 24 million dinars ($4 million) alone in social security compensations, including child allowance.
Another powerful election tool now at Zajedno's disposal in Nis and Kragujevac is the local media which the Socialists tried and failed to wrest from their control.

Head of the Kragujeva electronic media Vidosav Stevanovic has promised to tell his audience the "truth about the sorry state of affairs" in their city and elsewhere in the republic, which voters have never heard from the state media.
